label: A Historical Interlude
notes: Welcome the class to the one history chapter of the book and frame its thesis at once: a disputed axiom only becomes a decidable mathematical question once you can build a model of its negation inside a trusted geometry. Promise that we will keep the geometry concrete with the Klein disk and the absolute conic.

label: Euclid's Five Postulates
notes: Walk through the first four postulates as the uncontroversial backbone, then dwell on the fifth. Stress that its wordiness and non-self-evidence are exactly why, for two thousand years, geometers believed it ought to be a theorem rather than an assumption, and tried to derive it from the other four.

label: The Fifth Is a Branch Point
notes: Use the dependency graph to make the key structural point: the fifth postulate is not isolated but logically equivalent to many familiar facts. Pick out Playfair's axiom and the triangle angle sum of pi as the equivalents we will test, so students see that denying one denies all of them together.

label: Centuries of Failed Proofs
notes: Tell the story of the failed proofs as productive failures. Each attempt smuggled in an assumption equivalent to the postulate. Saccheri's reductio is the turning point: he derived strange but contradiction-free theorems from the acute hypothesis and only rejected them on aesthetic grounds, missing the discovery by a hair.

label: Saccheri and Lambert Quadrilaterals
notes: Define the Saccheri quadrilateral carefully: two equal sides perpendicular to a base, and the two summit angles necessarily equal. The whole nineteenth-century question collapses into a single trichotomy about those summit angles. Draw the figure on the board and label the three hypotheses before revealing which geometry each one names.

label: Three Hypotheses, Three Geometries
notes: Connect the trichotomy to angle sums and curvature. Right summit angles give Euclidean flatness and angle sum exactly pi; obtuse angles give elliptic geometry where lines always meet; acute angles give hyperbolic geometry with angle sum below pi. Emphasize that the acute case is internally consistent, not absurd.

label: Gauss, Bolyai, Lobachevsky
notes: Recount the independent triple discovery. Gauss kept his results private, fearing controversy; the young Bolyai published his appendix; Lobachevsky developed the system most fully in print. Stress that all three accepted the acute hypothesis as a real geometry and explored it deductively, decades before anyone proved it consistent.

label: The Angle of Parallelism
notes: Introduce Lobachevsky's angle of parallelism as the quantitative signature of the new geometry. Through a point off a line there are two limiting parallels making an acute angle that depends on distance and shrinks toward zero far away. In Euclid this angle is always a right angle, so this formula encodes the postulate's failure.

label: The Beltrami-Klein Disk
notes: Now build the model that ends the debate. Points are interior to the unit circle, lines are straight chords, and the circle itself is the absolute conic representing points at infinity. Show many chords through a point all missing a given chord, making Playfair's axiom visibly false inside an ordinary Euclidean picture.

label: Distance from the Absolute
notes: Explain how the boundary supplies a metric. The two ideal endpoints of a chord, together with the two interior points, form a cross-ratio whose logarithm is the hyperbolic distance. This is the Cayley-Klein construction: distance is measured projectively relative to the chosen absolute conic, and the boundary sits infinitely far away.

label: Consistency via Models
notes: State the punchline as a logician would. Because every hyperbolic primitive translates into a verified statement about the Euclidean disk, any contradiction in hyperbolic geometry would force a contradiction in Euclidean geometry. So the two stand or fall together, and the parallel postulate is proven genuinely independent. Mention Poincare's conformal companion model.

label: One Absolute, Three Geometries
notes: Close by lifting everything to the Cayley-Klein viewpoint of the preceding chapters. Choosing a real absolute conic gives hyperbolic geometry, a degenerate one gives Euclidean, and an imaginary one gives elliptic. The history resolves into a single projective picture: each geometry is just measurement relative to a chosen absolute.
